transcript.question: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?
transcript.answer: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. My work involves adding new drones to our fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, and sending drones to charge. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back afterwards.

transcript.question: When you arrive at work at the start of your shift, what is the very first thing you do?
Who tells you what needs to be worked on when you start your day?
Could you tell me about the worst day you have had at work in the last few months?
What is something you currently check by hand because you do not trust automated information?
When you think about a new software system being introduced, what concerns or worries do you have about what it might do wrong?
transcript.answer: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about reports from drones arriving late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. I also worry that the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, meaning an instruction might get through twice and the sender often cannot tell if the first attempt arrived. Additionally, the service runs on a single server, gets updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes.

transcript.answer: I am a dispatcher, which means I plan and run the flights as the licensed person responsible for each one. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I also have the power to call off a flight.

transcript.question: When you sit down for a shift, how does your day typically begin?

transcript.answer: Software never chooses a drone for us because our policy forbids it, so I make that choice myself. As a dispatcher, I am legally responsible for picking the drone and the way it flies, though I do want help finding out which of our drones could get to where a job starts.

transcript.answer: I worry about a closure coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. I also worry about closures being announced suddenly or amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.

transcript.answer: My role at the airspace desk is to keep the shared picture of the airspace. This includes maintaining the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Since I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations, I want to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers when it is entered.

transcript.answer: When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

transcript.answer: The closure announcements come from the authorities. They define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once.
